client: I've been really anxious ever since my professor assigned this big group presentation project. The thought of having to speak in front of the whole class makes my stomach turn, and I'm already worrying about messing up or freezing during my part. I'm not sure how talking about it will help when the problem is that I just can't handle public speaking situations.
therapist: It sounds like this presentation is really stirring up some strong physical and emotional reactions for you. I hear how overwhelming the anticipation feels, and I wonder if we could explore what thoughts are running through your mind when you picture yourself giving this presentation?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: I keep imagining myself freezing up in front of everyone, my mind going completely blank. My chest gets tight just thinking about it, like I can't breathe. Part of me knows it's probably not going to be that bad, but the fear feels so real right now.
therapist: I notice that while you're describing this intense fear, there's also a part of you that recognizes it might not be as bad as it feels. That's an important observation. Let's explore that thought - what makes you believe it might not be as bad as you're imagining?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client:
I guess I know logically that most of my fears never actually happen, but it's like my brain keeps preparing for the worst-case scenario anyway. Even when I try to tell myself it's not that bad, the anxious feelings just take over and it's hard to shake them. 

Sometimes I worry that if I stop being anxious about things, I'll be caught off guard when something bad does happen. It's like my anxiety is trying to protect me, even though it mostly just makes me miserable.
therapist: You've described something really important - this idea that your anxiety is trying to protect you, even though it ends up causing distress. That's such a common human experience. Can you tell me more about how this protective mechanism shows up for you in everyday situations?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I notice it most when I'm about to meet new people or go to social events. My mind starts racing with all these "what if" scenarios - what if I say something stupid, what if they don't like me. Part of me knows it's irrational, but another part feels like this anxiety is somehow keeping me safe from rejection.
therapist: It sounds like you're caught between recognizing these thoughts may be exaggerated and feeling like they serve an important protective purpose. I'm curious - when you've faced social situations despite these worries, what have you noticed happens to those feared outcomes?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client:
I know logically that my fears are usually worse than reality, but it's hard to shake the feeling that if I let my guard down even once, something bad will happen. When I do push through and socialize, people are usually nice enough, but I still leave feeling exhausted from analyzing every interaction for mistakes I might have made. 

It's like my brain keeps saying "See? Nothing terrible happened THIS time, but what about next time?" The relief never lasts.
therapist: I hear how exhausting this cycle is for you - even when things go okay socially, your mind keeps scanning for potential threats. That sounds really draining. What do you make of the fact that your experiences keep showing the feared outcomes don't actually happen, yet the worry persists?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client:
I know logically that my fears usually don't come true, but it's like my brain won't accept that evidence. Even when a social event goes fine, I'll lie awake afterward picking apart every little thing I said wrong. It's like I can't trust that things will be okay next time. 

The worrying feels automatic, like I don't have control over it. I'll tell myself "see, nothing bad happened," but then the next time I'm in a social situation, the anxiety comes right back just as strong. It's frustrating because I know I'm being irrational, but that doesn't make the feelings go away.
therapist: I notice you're describing this frustrating pattern with such clarity and insight - recognizing how your mind keeps returning to worry despite evidence to the contrary. That awareness is actually an important first step. Would you be willing to explore what it might look like to gradually build more trust in your ability to handle social situations, even with some anxiety present?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client:
I guess I understand what you're saying about awareness being a first step, but it doesn't really make the anxiety go away in the moment. When I'm actually in social situations, all I can think about is how badly I might mess up or how people are judging me. It's easy to talk about trusting myself here in therapy, but out in the real world it feels impossible. 

I've tried positive thinking before and it just makes me feel worse when I still end up anxious. Like I'm failing at controlling my own mind.
therapist: I hear how frustrating it feels when the anxiety persists despite your best efforts - that sense of "knowing better" but still feeling overwhelmed in the moment. Rather than trying to force positive thinking, what if we explored how to make space for these anxious thoughts while still engaging in social situations?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I get what you're saying about making space for the anxious thoughts, but it's so hard when I'm actually in a social situation. My mind just races and I can't think straight - it's like the anxiety takes over completely. I worry people will notice how uncomfortable I am and judge me for it.
therapist: It sounds like in those social moments, the anxiety feels so all-consuming that it's hard to practice any of the tools we discuss here. That makes complete sense - our brains are wired to prioritize perceived threats. I wonder if we could explore what happens if, just for a moment, you notice the anxiety without trying to push it away or fix it?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I get what you're saying about noticing the anxiety, but when it hits me at parties or gatherings, it feels impossible to just observe it. My mind immediately jumps to "everyone can tell I'm freaking out" and I just want to escape. Doesn't noticing it make it worse? Like focusing on a fire instead of putting it out?
therapist: I hear how overwhelming that experience feels - like the anxiety demands all your attention and makes it hard to do anything else. You raise an important question about whether noticing it could make things worse, almost like giving the fire more fuel. What if we experimented with just briefly acknowledging the anxiety, then gently shifting focus to something in your surroundings?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, very quiet, moderate-paced speech

client:
I get what you're saying, but when I try to shift my focus, the anxiety just feels louder, like it's screaming "don't ignore me!" It's frustrating because I want to try your suggestion, but part of me worries that even acknowledging it for a second will make it spiral out of control. 

I had this happen yesterday when I was at the grocery store - I noticed my heart racing and tried to look at the products on the shelf, but then I just started worrying about having a panic attack in public.
therapist: It sounds like your experience in the grocery store was really distressing - like the harder you tried to shift away from the anxiety, the more it insisted on being heard. That must have felt exhausting. I wonder if we could explore what happens if we approach these moments with curiosity rather than resistance?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech
